**Title:** Metformin Use Is Associated With Reduced Rates of Primary Nerve Decompression Surgery and Revision in Type 2 Diabetes: A Retrospective Cohort Study.

**Authors:** Yamen Abbas, Amir Kucharski, Adam Boukind, David Wright, Christopher J Dy, David M Brogan

**Journal:** Journal of hand surgery global online
**Publication Date:** 2026-10-25
**DOI:** 10.1016/j.jhsg.2026.101148
**PMC ID:** 13695114
**Full Text Available:** Yes
**Full Text URL:** https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pmc/articles/PMC13695114/


**Abstract:**
Type 2 diabetes mellitus is a risk factor for compressive neuropathy. The purpose of this study was to determine whether metformin use is associated with reduced rates of compressive neuropathy, primary nerve decompression surgery, and revision after carpal tunnel release and cubital tunnel release, while controlling for concurrent diabetes medications.

**Full Text:**

Type 2 diabetes mellitus is a risk factor for compressive neuropathy. The purpose of this study was to determine whether metformin use is associated with reduced rates of compressive neuropathy, primary nerve decompression surgery, and revision after carpal tunnel release and cubital tunnel release, while controlling for concurrent diabetes medications.

We performed a retrospective cohort study using the TriNetX federated research network. Adults with type 2 diabetes mellitus were stratified by metformin exposure, defined as at least 10 prescriptions over 5 years. The primary outcomes were incident compressive neuropathy and nerve decompression surgery. In a unilateral revision cohort, the outcome was ipsilateral revision between 30 days and 5 years after the index procedure. One-to-one propensity score matching balanced cohorts on demographics, comorbidities, and concurrent diabetes medications. Four prespecified medication-stratified sensitivity analyses addressed insulin, sodium-glucose cotransporter-2 inhibitors, and glucagon-like peptide-1 receptor agonists. Carpal tunnel release and cubital tunnel release revision results were pooled via fixed-effect meta-analysis.

After matching, the primary analysis included 260,823 pairs. Metformin users had lower rates of nerve decompression surgery (0.60% vs 0.72%; odds ratio, OR, 0.831 [0.776–0.889]) and compressive neuropathy diagnosis (2.78% vs 3.05%; OR, 0.909 [0.879–0.941]). The surgery-level association was stronger without concurrent insulin (OR, 0.727 [0.662–0.799]) and attenuated to nonsignificance with concurrent insulin (OR, 0.948 [0.836–1.076]), though the diagnosis-level association persisted. Among patients with unilateral carpal or cubital tunnel syndrome, ipsilateral revision was less frequent in metformin users (pooled OR, 0.711 [0.533–0.950]). Metformin users also had lower vitamin B12 levels (mean, 646.4 vs 707.4 pg/mL), consistent with sustained metformin exposure.

Metformin use was associated with reduced incidence of nerve decompression surgery and ipsilateral revision after carpal tunnel release and cubital tunnel release in patients with type 2 diabetes mellitus, with directionally consistent effects across sensitivity analyses. These findings suggest that maintaining metformin therapy may carry benefit beyond glycemic control. Prospective studies are needed to validate these findings.

Key words: Carpal tunnel syndrome, Compressive neuropathy, Cubital tunnel syndrome, Metformin, Type 2 diabetes mellitus

Type 2 diabetes mellitus (T2DM) is an independent risk factor for development of compressive neuropathies, including carpal tunnel syndrome and ulnar neuropathy at the elbow.1 Patients with diabetes who undergo carpal tunnel release (CTR) also experience higher complication rates and are at greater risk of requiring revision surgery. In a 5-year Australian cohort of 1,287 patients, diabetes was associated with increased Clavien-Dindo grade IIIb complications,2 while analysis of a separate cohort demonstrated that diabetes independently predicted revision CTR within 1 year on multivariable analysis, alongside male sex, tobacco use, and endoscopic technique.3

Despite this well-documented burden, no study has examined whether metformin, one of the first-line agents for T2DM, influences the rate of compressive neuropathy, primary nerve decompression surgery, or subsequent revision surgery. In preclinical models, metformin has demonstrated neuroprotective properties, including anti-inflammatory effects in peripheral nerve, promotion of axonal regeneration, and neurotrophic factor upregulation.4, 5, 6 These effects are mediated in part through autophagy, a cellular degradation and recycling process,7,8 also modulated by other commonly prescribed T2DM medications, including insulin, sodium-glucose cotransporter-2 inhibitors (SGLT2i) and glucagon-like peptide-1 receptor agonists (GLP-1 RA).9, 10, 11 Investigating metformin's neuroprotective contribution therefore requires systematic control for these concurrent agents.

The purpose of this study was to determine whether metformin use is associated with reduced rates of compressive neuropathy, primary nerve decompression surgery, and revision after CTR and cubital tunnel release (CuTR) in patients with T2DM, while controlling for concurrent diabetes medications.

This retrospective cohort study used the TriNetX federated electronic health record research network, which aggregates deidentified data from more than 117 million patients across more than 80 United States health care organizations. TriNetX has been validated for pharmacoepidemiologic research and provides real-time access to diagnoses, procedures, medications, laboratory values, and demographics. This study was exempt from institutional review board approval because TriNetX provides deidentified patient data. This study was conducted and reported in accordance with the Strengthening the Reporting of Observational Studies in Epidemiology guidelines for cohort studies.

We identified adults (≥18 years) with a diagnosis of T2DM (International Classification of Diseases, Tenth Revision [ICD-10] code E11) between January 1, 2007, and December 31, 2020, with data available through 2025 to allow up to 5 years of follow-up after the index date. For the primary analysis, the T2DM diagnosis date served as the index. The unilateral revision cohort comprised patients with T2DM having unilateral carpal tunnel syndrome (CTS; ICD-10 G56.01 or G56.02) or unilateral cubital tunnel syndrome (CuTS; G56.21 or G56.22) who underwent ipsilateral CTR (Current Procedural Terminology [CPT] code 64721) or CuTR (CPT code 64718), with the date of the primary surgery as the index; patients with bilateral CTS (G56.03) were excluded. Patients with estimated glomerular filtration rate ≤30 mL/min/1.73 m2 or chronic kidney disease stage 4, stage 5, or end-stage renal disease were excluded as contraindications to metformin. Patients were stratified by metformin exposure status, defined as receiving at least 10 metformin prescriptions during the 5-year follow-up window after the index date. The control group comprised patients with T2DM meeting the same criteria with no metformin prescriptions in the same window. The most recent vitamin B12 laboratory levels within the 5-year follow-up window were compared between cohorts as a pharmacologic compliance signal for sustained metformin intake.

For the primary analysis cohort, outcomes were incident compressive neuropathy diagnosis (composite of CTS, CuTS, Guyon canal syndrome, or tarsal tunnel syndrome) and incident nerve decompression surgery (composite of CTR, CuTR, Guyon canal release, or tarsal tunnel release), assessed during the 5-year (1,825-day) follow-up window after the T2DM index date. Individual diagnoses and procedures were also analyzed. For each outcome, patients with a prior occurrence of that specific outcome before the index date were excluded from that outcome's analysis to restrict to incident events. For the unilateral revision cohort, the outcome was ipsilateral revision (same CPT code as the index procedure) occurring within 30 days to 5 years after the index surgery. The 30-day exclusion window eliminates staged or immediate revision procedures unrelated to treatment failure. The 5-year upper bound captures the majority of revision surgeries, as the median time to revision CTR is 2.5 years (interquartile range, 1.0–3.8 years),12 and the median time to revision CuTR is 1.2 years (interquartile range, 0.6–2.4 years).13

One-to-one propensity score matching without replacement was performed using a caliper of 0.1 standard deviations, based on age, sex (defined as biologic sex as recorded in the medical record), race/ethnicity, body mass index, hemoglobin A1c, diabetic neuropathy (E11.40–42), hypothyroidism, chronic kidney disease, nicotine dependence, concurrent diabetes medications (insulin, sulfonylureas, thiazolidinediones, dipeptidyl peptidase-4 inhibitors, GLP-1 receptor agonists, SGLT2 inhibitors), and additional comorbidities and concurrent medications. Postmatch covariate balance was evaluated using standardized mean differences as detailed in Table S1, available on the Journal’s website at www.jhsgo.org.

Four prespecified sensitivity analyses were designed to control for the effects of concurrent diabetes medications on the metformin and nonmetformin cohorts. Two analyses addressed insulin: one excluding insulin from both cohorts (No Insulin; pharmacologic subclass HS501 excluded from both cohorts) and one requiring insulin in both cohorts (Insulin Both; HS501 required in both cohorts). Two analyses addressed concurrent SGLT2i and GLP-1 RA use: at least one of these agents required in both cohorts (SGLT2i or GLP-1 RA in Both; Anatomical Therapeutic Chemical codes A10BK and/or A10BJ) and neither agent in either cohort (No SGLT2i or GLP-1 RA; Anatomical Therapeutic Chemical codes A10BK and A10BJ excluded from both cohorts). Because insulin and SGLT2i/GLP-1 RA have independent effects on the autophagy pathways implicated in metformin's proposed neuroprotective mechanism, the “No Insulin” and “No SGLT2i or GLP-1 RA” analyses provide more mechanistically isolated comparisons; the remaining analyses test whether metformin retains benefit alongside these agents.

Data availability statement: The data underlying this study were obtained from the TriNetX federated research network under a data use agreement and are not publicly available because of licensing restrictions and patient-privacy protections. Access to TriNetX data requires a separate agreement with TriNetX (https://trinetx.com).

For each comparison, odds ratios with 95% CIs were calculated, with statistical significance assessed using z-tests for the difference in proportions. Continuous laboratory values (vitamin B12) were compared using a two-sample t test. For the primary analysis cohort, composite end points were defined within the TriNetX platform; individual diagnoses and procedures were also analyzed. For the unilateral revision cohort, CTR and CuTR were analyzed separately and pooled via inverse-variance weighted fixed-effect meta-analysis, with heterogeneity quantified using the I2 statistic. A two-tailed P < .05 was considered significant. No formal adjustment for multiple comparisons was applied across the sensitivity analyses. The prespecified sensitivity analysis design mitigates but does not eliminate the risk of type I error, and individual drug class analyses should be interpreted as hypothesis-generating. Analyses were performed using the TriNetX platform and R (R Foundation for Statistical Computing, version 4.5.2).

After propensity score matching, 260,823 matched pairs were available for analysis. Metformin users had lower rates of nerve decompression surgery than controls (composite outcome of CTR, CuTR, Guyon canal release, or tarsal tunnel release: 0.60% vs 0.72%; OR, 0.831; 95% CI, 0.776–0.889; P < .001), with consistent direction across CTR (0.46% vs 0.55%; OR, 0.844; 0.782–0.912) and CuTR (0.14% vs 0.17%; OR, 0.817; 0.710–0.940). The same direction held at the diagnosis-level (composite CTS, CuTS, Guyon canal syndrome, or tarsal tunnel syndrome: 2.78% vs 3.05%; OR, 0.909; 0.879–0.941; P < .001). The Table 1 and Figure present results across all sensitivity analyses.

Squares represent ORs and horizontal lines represent 95% CIs; the dashed vertical line indicates OR = 1. ORs below 1 favor metformin.

The association between metformin and reduced compressive neuropathy varied by concurrent insulin use. In patients without concurrent insulin (n = 153,342 per cohort), metformin users had lower odds of nerve decompression surgery (OR, 0.727; 95% CI, 0.662–0.799; P < .001). This association was not significant when both the metformin and nonmetformin cohorts received insulin (n = 55,160 per cohort; OR, 0.948; 95% CI, 0.836–1.076; P = .410), though the diagnosis-level association remained significant (OR, 0.924; 0.866–0.985; P = .016).

A similar pattern was observed when stratifying by concurrent SGLT2i and/or GLP-1 RA use. The association was stronger without these agents (OR, 0.803; 95% CI, 0.739–0.873; P < .001) and attenuated when present in both cohorts (OR, 0.874; 95% CI, 0.778–0.981; P = .023), though the diagnosis-level association did not reach statistical significance (OR, 0.944; 0.883–1.008; P = .084).

Among patients with unilateral CTS who underwent CTR, metformin users had lower rates of ipsilateral revision than controls (2.8% vs 4.2%; OR, 0.653; 95% CI, 0.459–0.929; P = .017). In patients with unilateral CuTS who underwent CuTR, revision rates did not differ significantly between cohorts (3.5% vs 4.1%; OR, 0.848; 95% CI, 0.512–1.405; P = .521). When the CTR and CuTR results were pooled, metformin users had lower revision rates than controls (3.0% vs 4.2%; pooled OR, 0.711; 95% CI, 0.533–0.950; P = .021; I2 = 0%). Vitamin B12 levels were lower in metformin users than controls (mean, 646.4 vs 707.4 pg/mL; median, 518 vs 548 pg/mL; P < .001), a difference that was directionally consistent across all medication strata (Table S2, available on the Journal’s website at www.jhsgo.org).

Metformin use was associated with a 17% reduction in odds of incident nerve decompression surgery in patients with T2DM (composite OR, 0.831; 95% CI, 0.776–0.889; P < .001), with a concordant reduction at incident compression neuropathy diagnoses (composite OR, 0.909; P < .001), and a 29% reduction in odds of ipsilateral revision after an index procedure (pooled OR, 0.711; 0.533–0.950; P = .021).

The observed association may be explained by metformin's neuroprotective effects, several converging on autophagy associated pathways. Autophagy is essential for Schwann cell function, and its dysregulation contributes to diabetic neuropathy progression.7 In type 2 diabetic mice, metformin restored adenosine monophosphate-activated protein kinase (AMPK)-mediated autophagy and reduced oxidative stress in sciatic nerve.8 Metformin also suppresses nuclear factor kappa B-mediated neuroinflammation, an effect possibly secondary to autophagy induction or a parallel pathway, and promotes axonal regeneration through neurotrophic factor upregulation and M2 macrophage polarization.4, 5, 6 In carpal tunnel syndrome, AMPK activation reduced collagen deposition and fibrotic remodeling in subsynovial connective tissue cells in vitro.14 Propensity-matched metformin users had lower tibial nerve cross-sectional area, reduced neuropathy symptoms, and superior neurophysiological function,15 and higher corneal nerve fiber density with lower dendritic cell density, suggesting reduced neuroinflammation.16

With insulin stratification, metformin's protective association was stronger without concurrent insulin and attenuated to nonsignificance at the surgery-level with insulin in both cohorts, although the diagnosis-level association persisted. Insulin suppresses autophagy through mechanistic target of rapamycin activation, potentially counteracting metformin's AMPK-mediated autophagy induction.9 This pharmacological antagonism may explain the observed attenuation. However, insulin-requiring patients also have more advanced diabetes with greater baseline nerve compromise, and the attenuation is therefore likely multifactorial.

A parallel gradient emerged with SGLT2i/GLP-1 RA stratification, the association being strongest when these agents were absent from both cohorts and attenuated when present. These agents independently activate autophagy in peripheral nerve of diabetic rodents and in Alzheimer's and Parkinson's models, through both AMPK-dependent and AMPK-independent mechanisms.10,11 The resulting overlap in autophagy-mediated neuroprotection may partially reduce the detectable metformin-specific effect. When both cohorts received these agents, the surgery-level association remained significant (OR, 0.874; 95% CI, 0.778–0.981; P = .023), although the diagnosis-level association did not reach significance (OR, 0.944; 0.883–1.008; P = .084). Both classes independently improve peripheral nerve excitability, neuropathy scores, small nerve fiber regeneration, and carpal tunnel syndrome incidence.17, 18, 19, 20

The metformin neuroprotection hypothesis is not universally supported. In the Copenhagen Insulin and Metformin Therapy (CIMT) randomized controlled trial, metformin was associated with increased orthostatic blood pressure drop relative to placebo, suggesting an adverse effect on cardiovascular autonomic neuropathy; no effect on vibration detection threshold was observed.21 That neuropathy involves autonomic small fibers mechanistically distinct from the motor and sensory fibers affected by entrapment neuropathies, limiting generalizability to compressive neuropathy. In the Diabetes Prevention Program and its Outcomes Study, metformin reduced diabetes incidence over 15 years, but the aggregate microvascular outcome did not differ from placebo.22 That study enrolled patients with prediabetes having lower neuropathy burden than our T2DM surgical cohort.

Su et al23 used TriNetX target trial emulation to compare SGLT2i and GLP-1 RA users, finding SGLT2 is associated with lower carpal tunnel syndrome incidence and lower CTR rates, though that study did not examine metformin. Seddio et al24 studied semaglutide in patients with CTR and found reduced short-term complications but similar reoperation rates. Shabbir et al25 found GLP-1 RA use associated with fewer reoperations and less frequent neuropathy diagnoses after cubital tunnel release. Snee et al26 examined metformin and painful neuroma formation after lower extremity amputation but found no significant metformin effect.

Among patients with unilateral CTS or CuTS, metformin use was associated with reduced ipsilateral revision, driven primarily by reduced revision CTR. Diabetes is an established risk factor for revision CTR. Carroll et al3 found that diabetes independently predicted revision within one year, and Zieske et al27 documented that recurrent carpal tunnel syndrome requiring revision was associated with a higher prevalence of diabetes. The higher event rates in our cohort reflect the T2DM population and longer outcome window.

Lower vitamin B12 levels in the metformin cohort may serve as a pharmacologic compliance proxy, suggesting sustained exposure. Vitamin B12 reduction is a well-established adverse effect of long-term metformin use; de Jager et al28 demonstrated a 19% decrease in vitamin B12 levels over 4.3 years in a placebo-controlled trial, and a meta-analysis of randomized trials reported a pooled reduction of 73 pg/mL.29 In our cohorts, metformin users had lower vitamin B12 levels (mean, 646.4 vs 707.4 pg/mL; P < .001), concordant with this established magnitude and consistent with sustained rather than isolated exposure. This suggests the observed protective association may be conservative, as metformin-associated vitamin B12 deficiency would be expected to worsen neuropathy outcomes, biasing results toward the null.30,31

These data do not support prescribing metformin solely for the purpose of reducing subsequent nerve release surgery. They do suggest that for T2DM patients with or at risk for compressive neuropathy, maintaining metformin therapy may carry neuroprotective benefit beyond glycemic control.

This study has several limitations. TriNetX does not encode procedure laterality; ipsilateral revision was operationalized as a repeat of the index CPT code in patients restricted to unilateral CTS or CuTS, mitigating but not excluding misclassification of a contralateral procedure as revision. Indication bias may inflate the protective association. Metformin is contraindicated in renal impairment (estimated glomerular filtration rate, less than 30 mL/min/1.73 m2), excluding patients with advanced nephropathy and higher neuropathy risk. Unmeasured confounders, including surgical technique, surgeon volume, and symptom severity, cannot be controlled. Because exposure required at least 10 metformin prescriptions, exposed patients had to remain in care to qualify, raising possible immortal-time bias and exposure misclassification. The vitamin B12 signal cannot confirm adherence or distinguish continuous from intermittent use. No adjustment for multiple comparisons was applied; individual drug class analyses are hypothesis-generating. CuTR analyses flagged incomplete data return from some organizations. The retrospective observational design precludes causal inference.

Maintaining metformin therapy may carry benefit beyond glycemic control in patients with T2DM having compressive neuropathy; prospective studies with nerve conduction data, adherence verification, and standardized surgical indications are needed to validate these findings.
